q: Why add NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK rules in the database when your app already validates?
options: Every path into the table goes through the same rules, and app code will have bugs
Database rules make queries run faster
App validation does not work with Postgres
Postgres requires at least one rule per table
why: Scripts, other services and bugs all write to your tables. Postgres says no to bad data itself.

options: As float, because it has decimals
As bigint cents, or numeric
As text, so nothing is rounded
As real, because it uses less space
why: Floats guess. Cents in a bigint are exact.

options: The date and time exactly as typed, with no zone
Only the time zone name
One moment in time, kept in UTC and shown in your session's time zone
A text label that you must convert yourself
why: Use timestamptz by default. In Prisma, ask for `@db.Timestamptz(3)` on purpose, because the default has no time zone.

q: A column has `DEFAULT 'pending'`. Your code runs `INSERT ... VALUES (NULL)` for that column. What is saved?
options: 'pending', because NULL means no value
An empty text ''
The previous row's value
NULL, or an error if the column is NOT NULL. The default is not used
why: No value means DEFAULT. NULL is a value. In Prisma, `undefined` leaves the field out, and `null` sends NULL.

q: You will filter, sort and add up a field. Should it live inside a JSONB column?
options: No. Use a normal column. JSONB is for shapes that change
Yes, JSONB is always faster
Yes, because JSONB is indexed automatically
No, because JSONB cannot store numbers
why: Filter, sort, join or add it up? Use a normal column.

q: An INSERT is refused by a CHECK rule. Does the id counter (the sequence) go back?
options: Yes, the counter goes back by one
No. The row is not saved, but the counter has already moved, so ids can have gaps
Yes, but only inside a transaction
The counter resets to 1
why: A refused row saves nothing, but the id counter still moves. So never expect ids without gaps.
